input:
A vapour-compression refrigeration unit serves an ice rink, evaporating at −10 °C and condensing at 40 °C. It is instructive to begin with the ideal benchmark for such a duty. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures works out to 5.26, and it is important to appreciate that this value represents a ceiling: it holds for a fully reversible machine operating between the same two temperatures, and no real unit working between the same temperatures can ever be expected to reach it.

In practice, the installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of just 2.4. This achieved value is taken from the manufacturer's test conducted at full load. It stands well below the ceiling because the real cycle inevitably spends the ideal margin: the compression is not reversible, the expansion takes place as a throttling rather than as a work-producing step, and each exchanger requires a finite temperature difference in order to pass its duty. It should also be noted that part-load performance is not stated, and the figure should not be extended to part-load operation.

Taken together, the two figures serve to fix the scale of the losses involved. At full load, the unit returns less than half of the refrigeration per unit of work that a reversible machine between the same temperatures would return, and any duty estimate for the rink at full load should accordingly be made with the measured figure rather than with the theoretical bound. What the bound additionally provides is a useful check: any claimed performance above it, for these temperatures, would be wrong on its face.
